claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5–1.0 at.% interstitial carbon or nitrogen to a Co–Cr–Ni or similar multicomponent alloy will induce short-range chemical order.
Adding approximately 0.5–1.0 at.% interstitial carbon or nitrogen will induce stabilized nanoscale precipitates.
The proposed short-range order or nanoprecipitates will refine the alloy microstructure.
The proposed short-range order or nanoprecipitates will reduce stacking-fault energy.
The proposed structural changes will promote beneficial interactions involving dislocations and deformation twins.
Interstitial additions locally modify lattice parameters.
Short-range ordering impedes dislocation motion in a controlled manner.
Activation of multiple deformation pathways, including partial-dislocation slip and twinning, can support concurrent strengthening and ductility.
Interstitial additions will enhance yield strength beyond that of the undoped baseline.
Interstitial additions will enhance ductility beyond that of the undoped baseline.
Interstitial additions will enhance Young's modulus beyond that of the undoped baseline.
Interstitial additions will enhance fracture toughness beyond that of the undoped baseline.
The doped alloy will exhibit at least a 10% increase in yield strength relative to the undoped alloy.
Any ductility loss caused by doping will be no greater than 5%.
Fracture toughness after doping will be comparable to or better than that of the baseline.
Young's modulus after doping will increase moderately or remain comparable to that of the baseline.
Current CrCoNi-based or similar HEAs and MEAs typically have yield strengths of approximately 700–1000 MPa.
Current CrCoNi-based or similar HEAs and MEAs typically have ductility of approximately 50–60%.
Interstitial concentrations above approximately 1 at.% may form coarse carbides or nitrides and cause premature fracture.
Atom-probe tomography can measure species-specific short-range order and monitor heat-treatment-induced SRO changes in CoCrNi.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis says ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture toughness will all be enhanced beyond the baseline, whereas the predicted outcome permits up to a 5% ductility loss and merely comparable modulus or fracture toughness.

The predicted outcome accepts limited ductility loss and comparable toughness, but the falsification rule asks for simultaneous improvement in strength and toughness or ductility; thus an outcome allowed by the prediction could also be classified as falsifying.
